attributes.title: Level 5

subgroups.name: build 1

steps.hints: ❓Did you select [left] or [right] in the two <is button pressed> value blocks?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:

Ask the ninja:

❓ How is using the <is button pressed> value block different from using the [on button pressed] container?

❓ What happens when you use a [forever] loop in a project? Why is it useful for this chunk of code?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 The <is button pressed> value block acts as a Boolean by checking whether a certain condition is true (whether a certain block is pressed). The [on button pressed] container acts as an event and causes something to happen when a certain button is pressed.
steps.instructions:
Set the Player sprite to face left or right depending on the direction it’s moving! 


From Controller, drag an <is button pressed> value block into the <true> value of both [if then] conditionals inside the [forever] loop. Click the drop down and select [left] or [right] depending on which way the sprite is facing. 


Click ▶ to see the Player sprite face left or right depending on which direction button is pressed.

steps.hints: ❓Did you set the Food sprite’s lifespan to a random number between 2 and 5 seconds using milliseconds (ms)?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:

Ask the ninja:

❓ What do 2 and 5 seconds look like as milliseconds?

❓ What do you think the snowflakes will be used for in this project?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡If they prefer, the ninja can simply duplicate the Player sprite’s [place sprite on top of random tile] block, select the Food sprite’s name, and move it below the Food sprite’s [set sprite to] block.

💡Remind the ninja that they can convert values from seconds to milliseconds by multiplying by 1000. In this case, 2 seconds is equal to 2000 milliseconds, and 5 seconds is equal to 5000 milliseconds.
steps.instructions:
Set the Food sprite to appear only on white tiles for a limited amount of time! 


Drag a [place sprite on top of random tile] block underneath the Food sprite’s [set sprite to] block. Select the name of the Food sprite, and the white tile.


Open Sprites and drag out a [set sprite [x]] block under the [place sprite on top of random tile] block. Select the name of the Food sprite, and click the dropdown to select [lifespan]. Drag a (pick random) block into the parameter of the Food sprite’s lifespan. Set it to pick a random number between 2 and 5 seconds.


Click ▶ to see the Food sprite in the tilemap before it disappears!

steps.hints: ❓Did you create a makeSnowflake function and define the function with blocks from the [on start] container?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:

Ask the ninja:

❓How does a function make it easier to code the same chunk of code multiple times in a project?

❓ Did you define the makeSnowflake function using a function container and call the function using a [call function] block?

❓How can you create a function call block in a project?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Guide the ninja through the process of selecting the Functions code block menu and creating a new function. Help them notice the pop up window, type in a descriptive name for their function, and then find the new function container on the editor.

💡 Point out to the ninja that there are multiple ways to create a function call block in a project. Once a function has been defined, a function call block will appear in the Functions code block menu which can be dragged into the editor. Alternatively, the ninja can right click on the function definition block in the editor, then select “Create ‘call _______” to create the function call block.
steps.instructions:
Create a function to reuse the Food sprite’s code. 


Click Advanced to open Functions, then select [Make a Function...]. Name the function makeSnowflake, then click Done.


Drag the Food sprite’s [set sprite to], [place sprite on top of random tile], and [set sprite lifespan] blocks into the [function makeSnowflake] container. 


Open Function and drag out a [call makeSnowflake] block into the [on start] container.


Click ▶ to see the Food sprite appear on the tilemap.

steps.hints: ❓Did you set the sprite kind to Food in the [on destroyed] container?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:

Ask the ninja:

❓Why would you want to call the makeSnowflake function in both the [on start] and [on destroyed] containers?

❓ Why is using the [call makeSnowflake] block more useful than duplicating all of the snowflake sprite’s code and placing it in the [on destroyed] container?

❓How can you create a function call block in a project?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Point out to the ninja that functions enable a project to reuse a chunk of code multiple times, more easily. By using the function blocks, the code is simplified, more organized, and easier to read.

💡 Point out to the ninja that there are multiple ways to create a function call block in a project. Once a function has been defined, a function call block will appear in the Functions code block menu which can be dragged into the editor. Alternatively, the ninja can right click on the function definition block in the editor, then select “Create ‘call _______” to create the function call block.
steps.instructions:
Call the makeSnowflake function again so the Food Sprite reappears after the Player sprite “catches” it. 


Drag out an [on destroyed] container and update the sprite kind to Food. Right click on the [function makeSnowflake] container and select “Create ‘call makeSnowflake”, then drag the [call makeSnowflake] block into the [on destroyed] container. 


Click ▶ to see the Food sprite reappear in a new tile location after the Player Sprite “catches” it.

steps.hints: ❓Did you place a [change score by] block in the [on (Player) overlaps (Food)] container?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:

Ask the ninja:

❓ What might the score be used for in this project?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Prompt the ninja to consider other uses for the score variable. In the next step, they will create levels for this project, based on the number of points earned by the Player sprite.
steps.instructions:
Code the score to increase when the Player sprite catches the Food sprites that appear on screen!


Set the score in the [on start] container and change the score in the [on (Player) overlaps (Food)] container.


Click ▶ to catch snowflakes and earn points!

steps.hints:
❓Did you name the function setLevel and the parameter level?

﻿❓Did you move the [set tilemap to] blocks to the correct [if then] conditional opening?

﻿
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:


Ask the ninja:

❓ How is a function with a parameter different than a function without a parameter?

❓ What will happen once Level 1 is reached? When Levels 2 and 3 are reached?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡Confirm the Ninja has used camelCase to name the function setLevel and the parameter level. Double check that the tilemap level shown in each comment matches the condition being checked for in the [function setLevel] container.

💡Point out to the ninja where they can find the code comments on each block. The ninja can look for the small post it note icon (found on the left side of the block) to minimize and maximize the comments. Confirm that the tilemap asset names match the code comments and the order of the [if/else if/else] conditional. Tilemap asset names can be found by opening the asset and looking in the bottom right corner.

💡Guide the ninja through the process of creating a new function with a parameter. Help them select a parameter, name the function and its parameter, and then identify the new function container on the editor.
steps.instructions:
Create different levels of this game. 


Create another function named setLevel. Click “Number” at the top of the pop up window to add a parameter. Name the parameter level, then click Done.


Drag an [if then] conditional into the setLevel function container, then click + 2 times. Drag a <0=0> comparison block into both <> spaces of the conditional. Click and drag the (level) parameter bubble into the left parameter of both <0=0> comparison blocks, then type “1” and “2” in the right parameters. 


Drag the 3 different level [set tilemap to] blocks from the [on start] container into the correct spot inside the conditional. Each [set tilemap to] block has a comment that tells which level it is for.

steps.hints: ❓Did you use the (join) value block in the [show long text] block?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:


Ask the ninja:

❓ What should appear on the screen in the dialog box?

❓ What value do you think the (level) parameter bubble will pull from?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡Remind the ninja to double check the sequence and formatting in the (join) value block. Encourage the ninja to test out the project to make sure that the text appears as they intended.
steps.instructions:
Tell the player which level they are on!


Drag a [show long text] block into the function container, underneath the conditional. Use a (join) value block to join the string “Level ” with the (level) parameter bubble to make the dialog box show the level number on screen. Be sure to include a space after the word Level in the string!

steps.hints: ❓Did you use a [call setLevel] block in the first 2 else if conditions to call different levels of the game?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:

﻿


Ask the ninja:

❓What block needs to be added to tell the function code when to run?

❓Did you input the correct values in each of the <0=0> comparison blocks and [call setLevel] blocks?

❓How can you create a function call block in a project?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Guide the ninja through the logic of the [if then] conditional in the [on (Player) overlaps (Food)] container. When the project begins, the game is set to Level 1 (and the function code is run). When the Player sprite reaches 5 points, the function code is called again, and changes the tilemap displayed and dialog box shown. This repeats again once the Player sprite reaches 10 points.

💡 Point out to the ninja that there are multiple ways to create a function call block in a project. Once a function has been defined, a function call block will appear in the Functions code block menu which can be dragged into the editor. Alternatively, the ninja can right click on the function definition block in the editor, then select “Create ‘call _______” to create the function call block.
steps.instructions:
Use the function parameter to call the different levels of the game!


Drag a [call setLevel] block into the [on start] container. The [call setLevel] block has a parameter that provides more information to the function, and should be set to 1 here. 


Drag an [if then] conditional into the [on sprite overlaps sprite] container. Click (+) 3 times on the conditional to create 3 if/else if conditions. Click (-) to remove the final else condition. 


Replace the conditionals’ <true> values with <0=0> comparison blocks, and drag a (score) bubble into each block’s left parameter.


Drag a [call setLevel] block inside the first if opening, then update the parameter to 2. Set the comparison block to change to the new level when the score is equal to 5. Repeat this step in the second else if condition, to pass 3 to the setLevel function, when the score is equal to 10.


Click ▶ to see the levels change as the score increases!

steps.hints: ❓Did you add a [use effect] block above the [game over] block to add a WIN effect?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:

Ask the ninja:

❓ What happens when the Player sprite reaches 15 points? 

❓ Why isn’t a [call function] block used in the third [if then] conditional?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Help the ninja notice that there are multiple code blocks found within the [function setLevel] container that is run multiple times, whereas in the third condition, there is only one block that runs one time, when the game ends.
steps.instructions:
Code the end of the game!


Drag a [game over] block inside the final else if condition inside the [on sprite overlaps sprite] container. Use another <0=0> comparison block and (score) bubble so the game is won when the score is equal to 15. Set the game over effect, too.


Click ▶ to see all 3 levels and win the game!

steps.hints: ❓Did you add customizations to your project, such as dialog boxes, splash screens, or effects?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:


Ask the ninja:

❓ What directions might help a user understand how to play the game?

❓ What other customizations might you add to this project? 


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡Guide ninjas to note that while these customizing blocks are open ended and not required for the game to “work”, they really improve the Player’s experience playing a game, either by giving context to what the Player should do or not do, or to provide a more fun experience overall. They also allow the Ninja to add their personal touch and express themselves through small details present in the game.
steps.instructions:
Customize this project by adding game directions with a dialog box or splash screen!


Click ▶ to see the completed project!

subgroups.introduction: Create a project that uses functions with a parameter to set different levels in a game.

validationItems.text: Set the Player sprite image to face left or right depending on which direction button is pressed.
Set the Food sprite to appear on a random tile and use a random number to set the lifespan.
Define a makeSnowflake function to create a Food sprite, then call the Food sprite in the [on start] and [on destroyed] containers
Set the score and increase it when the Player sprite overlaps the Food sprite.
Define a setLevel function with a parameter that uses a conditional to create multiple levels.
Use a dialog box to display the current level number.
Call the setLevel function with different parameters to change the level based on the score.
Code the end of the game when the score is equal to 15.
Use a dialog box to provide game instructions.

attributes.description: You’ve reached Level 5 of Orange Belt! Before you create your final Orange Belt project, there are a few neat tricks to learn that could take your game to the next level! In this level, you’ll learn more about functions, which are chunks of code that run whenever they are called. You’ll learn how to create your own functions to simplify code and make something happen multiple times in a project. Here are the achievements you’ll unlock in Level 5:

badges.title: Function Junction
badges.description: Create functions, with and without parameters, to make something happen in a project.

badges.title: Make Your Own Way
badges.description: Create a new function to be used in a project.

badges.title: Don't Forget To Call
badges.description: Call a user-created function in a project.

badges.title: Customize Your Own Way
badges.description: Create a new function that takes a parameter to be used in a project.

badges.title: Area Code
badges.description: Call a user-created function that takes a parameter in a project.
